subject: Biology
name: Biology, Year 12
about: HSC, Heredity, genetic change and disease
syllabus: NSW Biology Stage 6 Syllabus (2017), Year 12 course, Modules 5 to 8

points.title: Sexual and asexual reproduction
points.brief: Asexual reproduction makes identical offspring from one parent and is fast. Sexual reproduction combines genes from two parents and gives variation.

points.title: Reproduction in plants, fungi and bacteria
points.brief: Flowering plants use pollination and seeds, fungi reproduce with spores and budding, and bacteria divide by binary fission.

points.title: Fertilisation and implantation in mammals
points.brief: A sperm and egg fuse to form a zygote, which divides and implants in the wall of the uterus.

points.title: Hormones in pregnancy
points.brief: Hormones such as progesterone and oestrogen keep the uterus lining in place and support the pregnancy. The placenta makes some of them.

points.title: Mitosis
points.brief: Division that makes two identical cells for growth and repair, keeping the full chromosome number.

points.title: Meiosis
points.brief: Division that makes four sex cells with half the chromosome number. Crossing over and independent assortment create variation.

points.title: DNA structure
points.brief: DNA is a double helix of two strands of nucleotides. Bases pair A with T and C with G, held by hydrogen bonds.

points.title: DNA replication
points.brief: The helix unzips and each strand is a template for a new one, so each copy has one old and one new strand.

points.title: Making proteins
points.brief: In transcription, a gene's DNA is copied into mRNA. In translation, ribosomes read the mRNA in codons and tRNA brings the matching amino acids to build a polypeptide.

points.title: Genotype and phenotype
points.brief: The genotype is the alleles an organism carries. The phenotype is the trait that shows, which also depends on the environment.

points.title: Dominant and recessive alleles
points.brief: A dominant allele shows when only one copy is present. A recessive one shows only with two copies. Punnett squares predict the ratios of offspring.

points.title: Codominance and incomplete dominance
points.brief: In codominance both alleles show fully, as in AB blood. In incomplete dominance the result is a blend, such as pink flowers from red and white.

points.title: Sex-linked inheritance
points.brief: Genes on the X chromosome, such as for red-green colour blindness, show more often in males, who have only one X.

points.title: Pedigrees
points.brief: Family trees that track a trait through generations, used to work out whether it is dominant, recessive or sex-linked.

points.title: Variation in populations
points.brief: Allele frequencies describe how common each version of a gene is in a population. Genetic testing and DNA sequencing show this variation.

points.title: Point and chromosomal mutations
points.brief: A point mutation changes one or a few bases. A chromosomal mutation changes part or all of a chromosome, such as a deletion or duplication.

points.title: Causes of mutation
points.brief: Mutations can happen by chance during copying, or be caused by mutagens such as ultraviolet light, radiation and some chemicals.

points.title: Somatic and germline mutations
points.brief: Somatic mutations happen in body cells and are not inherited. Germline mutations happen in sex cells and can be passed on.

points.title: Coding and non-coding DNA
points.brief: Only a small part of DNA codes for proteins. Non-coding DNA includes regions that control when genes are switched on.

points.title: Gene flow and genetic drift
points.brief: Gene flow moves alleles between populations. Genetic drift is chance change in allele frequencies, strongest in small populations.

points.title: What biotechnology is
points.brief: Using living things or their parts to make products, from bread and cheese to medicines made by modified bacteria.

points.title: Reproductive technologies
points.brief: Artificial insemination, artificial pollination and IVF let people choose which organisms breed, in farming and in medicine.

points.title: Cloning
points.brief: Making genetically identical copies of genes, cells or whole organisms, as with plant cuttings or the cloning of Dolly the sheep.

points.title: Recombinant DNA and transgenic organisms
points.brief: Cutting a gene from one organism and inserting it into another, such as the human insulin gene into bacteria, to make a transgenic organism.

points.title: Effects of biotechnology on biodiversity
points.brief: Genetic engineering and selective breeding can narrow genetic diversity in crops and livestock, which can make them vulnerable to new diseases.

points.title: Ethics of biotechnology
points.brief: Biotechnology raises questions of safety, fairness, ownership of genes and changing nature, and different groups weigh them differently.

points.title: Types of pathogens
points.brief: Prions, viruses, bacteria, protozoa, fungi and parasites cause disease in different ways. Viruses need a host cell to reproduce.

points.title: Koch's postulates
points.brief: Koch's steps link a particular microbe to a disease, by finding it in sick hosts, growing it and showing it causes the disease in a healthy host.

points.title: Pasteur and germ theory
points.brief: Pasteur's experiments, including swan-neck flasks, showed microbes come from other microbes, not from nowhere, and cause decay and disease.

points.title: How diseases spread
points.brief: Diseases spread by direct contact, droplets, contaminated food or water, and vectors such as mosquitoes.

points.title: Plant responses to pathogens
points.brief: Plants have physical barriers, such as thick cell walls, and chemical defences, and can kill infected cells to stop a pathogen spreading.

points.title: The first line of defence
points.brief: Skin, mucous membranes, cilia, stomach acid and tears stop most pathogens getting in.

points.title: The innate immune response
points.brief: Inflammation, fever and phagocytes, which engulf pathogens, respond quickly to any invader in the same way.

points.title: The adaptive immune response
points.brief: B cells make antibodies that bind particular antigens. T cells kill infected cells or help other immune cells. This response is slower but targeted.

points.title: Immune memory
points.brief: Memory cells stay after an infection, so a second exposure to the same pathogen brings a faster, stronger response.

points.title: Vaccination
points.brief: A vaccine exposes the body to a harmless form or part of a pathogen, so memory cells form without illness.

points.title: Herd immunity
points.brief: When enough people are immune, a pathogen cannot spread easily, which protects people who cannot be vaccinated.

points.title: Antibiotics and antivirals
points.brief: Antibiotics kill or stop bacteria and do nothing to viruses. Antivirals slow a virus. Overuse of antibiotics breeds resistant bacteria.

points.title: Epidemics and public health
points.brief: Quarantine, hygiene, clean water, contact tracing and tracking cases help stop outbreaks spreading locally and globally.

points.title: Aboriginal medicines and research
points.brief: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander knowledge of plants with medicinal uses has been studied by scientists, which raises questions of consent and fair sharing of benefits.

points.title: Homeostasis and negative feedback
points.brief: Homeostasis keeps internal conditions steady. In negative feedback, a change is detected and the response reverses it.

points.title: Controlling body temperature
points.brief: The hypothalamus detects temperature changes and triggers sweating, shivering and changes in blood flow to the skin.

points.title: Controlling blood glucose
points.brief: Insulin lowers blood glucose and glucagon raises it. Both are hormones made by the pancreas.

points.title: Water balance in the body
points.brief: The kidneys adjust how much water is lost in urine, under the control of a hormone called ADH.

points.title: Plant responses to stay in balance
points.brief: Plants control water loss by closing stomata and dropping leaves in drought.

points.title: Types of non-infectious disease
points.brief: Non-infectious diseases come from genes, the environment, nutrition or how cells grow, such as cystic fibrosis, skin cancer, scurvy and heart disease.

points.title: Epidemiology
points.brief: Studying patterns of disease in populations, through incidence, prevalence and mortality, to find causes and test treatments.

points.title: Prevention programs
points.brief: Programs such as skin cancer campaigns and screening find disease early or cut risk factors.

points.title: Technologies for hearing loss
points.brief: Hearing aids make sounds louder. Cochlear implants, developed in Australia, turn sound into electrical signals sent to the auditory nerve.

points.title: Technologies for vision and kidney disease
points.brief: Glasses, contact lenses and laser surgery correct vision. Dialysis filters the blood when the kidneys fail.
